name: Colin Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What fills an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Colin, 43, with a master’s in music. I lead the double-bass players in a theatre orchestra, record short bass lines for local adverts and teach four older pupils. The double bass is the tall string instrument that holds down the low notes. I can steady a section through a sudden change onstage; I still have to prepare every part. I like the small nod a conductor gives when we all land together, and I dislike an advert client calling a second use a small favour.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the family counting on from those fees?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner is a nurse with regular shifts, and our two children are in school. We have a mortgage, my music pay is high for this area, and about nine months of expenses are saved. There are plenty of other teaching and playing jobs nearby, though none is mine without a written offer. I have never used an AI tool and mark the rehearsal parts in pencil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the theatre that a cleaner booking list is fine if the paid rehearsal still happens. A bass section has to hear what the singers do in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nine months saved and my partner’s nurse wage cover an ordinary late advert payment. I still want a signed reuse fee, because a copied bass line can earn a client money twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the orchestra dates and four pupils this season. This week I’d ask the theatre for its paid rehearsal schedule and the advert client for written reuse terms, then save a fifth of any cleared extra recording fee after mortgage and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our income in this mild picture. A delayed recording cheque would irritate me, but it would not change the children’s supper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a client use a line twice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A client reused my bass opening for a second campaign last spring. I sent an invoice before recording another line for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use AI to keep the schedule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used an AI tool. The theatre can use one, but I will check paid dates against my paper contract.

do: Keep **orchestra dates** and four pupils this season.

feel: I feel **calm** because current paid work and savings cover ordinary delays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the theatre that generated advert bass lines may erase real paid sessions before robots can lift a bass. I would ask every client for a minimum fee and written limits on reusing my playing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Advert parts and arrangement work are roughly a quarter of my music income. If clients buy generated lines, I will still play shows, but the reserve cannot grow at the same pace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d compare the last ten advert invoices with new offers and ask the studio for minimum session and reuse terms. In the first year, if recording orders fall, I’d stop renting a separate practice room on empty weekdays and keep the paid orchestra and pupils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing my own recording money. Nine months saved buys time to look, but a bank balance cannot play a session for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try an AI bass line yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used an AI tool. I would ask to hear the finished track and read the client’s use terms before adding my own playing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the studio offers only a credit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a fee instead. A recording credit does not pay the mortgage or the person who tuned the bass before the take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the orchestra that thinking AGI by 2028 could make advert parts and schedules cheaply, while robots able to play a bass follow around 2031. I would ask for a signed season now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the advert lines to lose buyers in 2028 and the theatre may cut a few live dates too. Nine months saved gives us time, but I would notice a quarter of my pay missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I’d get written theatre dates and confirm four pupils’ next term. In the first year after AGI arrives, if advert orders stop and live dates shrink, I’d apply for an advertised school bass-teacher role only if it accepts my master’s and experience and written net pay after travel replaces lost income with confirmed school pickup; I’d keep the orchestra and pupils until a signed offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about my own fees, but not lost for choices. Several schools are near enough to ask, provided one actually posts a paid opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a lower-paid school title?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare actual teaching and preparation hours before leaving a paid stage. A title cannot settle the mortgage on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your partner cover school pickup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nursing shifts change, so I would confirm the rota or paid childcare before accepting afternoon hours. I would not promise a school my evenings without that.

I would ask for **signed theatre dates** before counting future pay.
think: I expect **advert lines** to lose buyers and live dates may shrink.

fieldNote: The **2028 advert loss** precedes robots able to play bass around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the theatre that five years lets us test whether a small live trio will earn its own fee. Thinking AGI could make advert lines around 2031, and capable bass-playing robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An independent wedding trio might replace recording money, but I will not ask a violinist or singer to rehearse for exposure. A signed booking is worth more than a full page of interest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I’d ask two players to try a separate wedding trio only after three couples sign and pay deposits. I’d accept those dates only if the deposits and written full fees cover the singer’s and violinist’s rehearsal and performance, my organising and playing time, travel and confirmed childcare; in the first year after 2031 I’d continue only while three paid bookings meet those terms, keeping orchestra shows that still pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about advert fees going within five years, although we can test three bookings without risking the mortgage reserve. A rehearsal called publicity is still unpaid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only one couple pays a deposit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would refund it and keep the existing orchestra dates. One wedding will not cover rehearsal for three players and childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would handle the contract?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put each musician’s share, rehearsal fee and cancellation term in one agreement. The other players should see that page before they commit a Saturday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my children that ten years is time to learn an instrument and ask what a rehearsal pays. Thinking AGI comes around 2036 and robot bass players around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I may still lead the bass section, but advert recordings could be worth less. Nine months saved and my partner’s wage make the next few years steady enough to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d keep orchestra dates and four pupils and save a fifth of each cleared extra advert fee after mortgage and food toward twelve months. Over the decade I’d run the separate trio only with three signed paid deposits and full written fees covering all players’ rehearsal and performance, my organising time, travel and confirmed childcare; in the first year after 2036 I’d keep it only while three paid bookings meet those terms and seek an advertised school role if advert fees end, provided my master’s qualifies and written net pay after travel replaces lost income with pickup covered, while retaining current work until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the far end of recording work, not the next mortgage payment. A decade helps me build a reserve and a real booking list, not wish for one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a van for the trio?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would use the transport we have while the written fees cover travel. I will not buy a vehicle against a forecast of weddings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a couple cancels?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The signed cancellation term must cover the musicians’ booked rehearsal time. If that term is missing, I will not reserve their Saturday.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because advert lines could disappear before another season is signed. Written theatre dates, a real school role with replacement net pay and three paid trio bookings would help. Nine months saved lets us search, but I will not spend it paying another musician to rehearse for free.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what a cancellation means to the players who held a Saturday. A wedding couple sees one booked Saturday; the musicians gave up three other offers to keep that date.

headlineQuote: A wedding couple sees one booked Saturday; the musicians gave up three other offers to keep that date.
portrait: Colin is a **43-year-old bass leader** with a music master’s, orchestra work, four pupils and advert recordings.
His **higher pay**, nurse partner, mortgage and nine-month reserve support two school-age children.
He **never uses AI** and relies on written session, reuse and cancellation fees.
Fast AGI threatens **advert fees** before robot players; he tests a separately paid trio and real school posts.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** could end advert pay before the orchestra signs another season.
whatWouldHelp: Written **theatre dates** and a posted school role with replacement net pay would help.
Three **paid trio bookings** covering all players and childcare could replace some recording income.
